gams

Splines

  • Piecewise regression yields continuous functions which are not, generally, smooth. Regression with splines yields smooth continuous functions.

  • A spline is essentially a Piecewise Polynomial but forces the ends of these pieces to meet perfectly smoothly so it looks like one continuous line.

  • A “spline” was a flexible strip of wood used by draftsmen to draw smooth curves through a set of points. We will do the same with several simple polynomial segments at specific points called knots

knots

We break the \(x\)-axis into multiple smaller regions. The specific points where we divide these regions are called knots.

Inside each region (between two knots), we fit a simple polynomial, usually a cubic (degree 3) function.

We must connect or touch each polynomial at the knot. Further, they must be smooth, non jerky transitions.

Build intuitions

Code 
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(splines) 
set.seed(123) 
n_points <- 100
x <- seq(-10, 10, length.out = n_points)
y <- sin(x / 1.5) * 1.5 + rnorm(n_points, sd = 0.3)
df <- data.frame(x = x, y = y)

knots <- c(-10, -5, 0, 5, 10)
segments_df <- data.frame(
  x_start = knots[-length(knots)], 
  x_end = knots[-1],     
  bin_id = factor(1:(length(knots) - 1)) 
)

segments_df$y_mean <- apply(segments_df, 1, function(row) {
  x_s <- as.numeric(row["x_start"])
  x_e <- as.numeric(row["x_end"])
  if (x_e == max(knots)) {
    in_bin <- df$x >= x_s & df$x <= x_e
  } else {
    in_bin <- df$x >= x_s & df$x < x_e
  }
  mean(df$y[in_bin], na.rm = TRUE)
})

segment_colors <- c("#377eb8", "#ff7f00", "#4daf4a", "#e41a1c")

ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = df, aes(x = x, y = y), color = "black", size = 2) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = knots, linetype = "Knot"), 
             color = "gray50", size = 0.8) +
  geom_segment(data = segments_df, 
               aes(x = x_start, xend = x_end, 
                   y = y_mean, yend = y_mean, 
                   color = bin_id), 
               size = 1.5) +
    scale_color_manual(values = segment_colors, guide = "none") + 
  scale_linetype_manual(name = "", values = c("Knot" = "dashed")) + 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-10, 10, 5), limits = c(-10.5, 10.5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(-2, 1, 1), limits = c(-2.2, 1.8)) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 20, hjust = 0.5),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 18),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 14),
    legend.position = c(0.85, 0.5), 
    legend.text = element_text(size = 16),
    legend.key.width = unit(1.5, "cm"), 
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

  • What does this equation look like?

  • We are transforming our X variable into multiple “synthetic” variables.

  • Right now, think of this as categorizing a continuous variable.

Code 
set.seed(123)
n_points <- 100
x <- seq(-10, 10, length.out = n_points)
y <- sin(x / 1.5) * 1.5 + rnorm(n_points, sd = 0.3)
df <- data.frame(x = x, y = y)
knots_all <- c(-10, -5, 0, 5, 10) 
knots_interior <- c(-5, 0, 5)
fit_linear <- lm(y ~ bs(x, knots = knots_interior, degree = 1), data = df)
df$pred_linear <- predict(fit_linear, newdata = df)

fit_cubic <- lm(y ~ bs(x, knots = knots_interior, degree = 3), data = df)
df$pred_cubic <- predict(fit_cubic, newdata = df)

create_spline_plot <- function(data, y_col, title, line_color) {
  ggplot(data, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
    geom_point(color = "black", size = 2) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = knots_all, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
    geom_line(aes_string(y = y_col), color = line_color, size = 1.5) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = knots_all, limits = c(-10.5, 10.5)) +
    labs(title = title, subtitle = "Vertical dashed lines = Knots") +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(size = 18, face = "bold"),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 14),
      axis.title = element_text(size = 14),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
    )
}

plot_linear <- create_spline_plot(df, "pred_linear", "Linear Spline (Degree 1)", "#377eb8")
plot_linear

  • How can we think of this equation? Same as before, but isntead of a 0,1 dummy varibale we are going to fit linear lines. Or similar to piecewise in that we are breaking up our predictor.

  • \[Y = B_{1}X_1 + B_{2}X_2 + B_{3}X_3 + \dots\]

Where \(X_1\) = x if x is between -10, & -5, zero for all else.

Where \(X_2\) = x if x is between -5, & 0, zero for all else.

** technically this is not what is happening, as this does not lead to having our ends of each segment meet one another, but this transformation is a good conceptual starting point **

\[y\sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\]

Standard regression: \[\mu = b_0+b_1 X_1\] Polynomial \[\mu = b_0+b_1 X_1+b_2X^2\] Splines/GAMs, where we have j synthetic variables, B. \[\mu = \beta_0 + \sum_{j=1}^{k} \beta_j B_j(X_i) \]

Basis Functions

\[f(x) = \sum_{j=1}^{k} \beta_j \cdot \text{Basis}_j(X_i)\]

  • Splines have Local effects rather than polynomials where the curve is across the entire range of X. To fit these local curves inbetween knots, we need to create a series of j basis functions to essential turn on and off the effect at different values of X across our different k knots.
Code 
library(splines)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)
x2 <- seq(0, 10, length.out = 100)
internal_knots <- c(2.5, 5, 7.5)
basis_mat <- bs(x2, knots = internal_knots, degree = 1, intercept = TRUE)
basis_df <- as.data.frame(basis_mat)
basis_df$x2 <- x2
colnames(basis_df)[1:(ncol(basis_df)-1)] <- paste0("Basis_", 1:(ncol(basis_df)-1))
basis_long <- pivot_longer(basis_df, 
                           cols = starts_with("Basis"), 
                           names_to = "Tent", 
                           values_to = "Value")
ggplot(basis_long, aes(x = x2, y = Value, color = Tent)) +
  geom_line(size = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(0, internal_knots, 10), 
             linetype = "dashed", color = "gray60") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1.1), breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.2)) +
  labs(title = "Linear B-Spline Basis Functions (Tents)",
       subtitle = "Notice how each tent peaks at 1.0 at its knot and is 0.0 at all other knots.",
       x = "Independent Variable (X)",
       y = "Basis Function Value (Membership)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Normal regression has 1 function

We will have number of basis functions equal to:

\(\text{Internal Knots} + \text{Degree} + \text{Intercept}\)

How do we get the estimates?

\[\hat{Y} = b_0+b_1 X_1\]

\[\hat{Y} = f(X)\]

\[ \hat{Y} = f(X) = \sum_{j=1}^{d}\beta_j \cdot \text{Basis}_j(X_i) \]

These basis functions become extra columns in your dataframe, just like your squared or cubed terms in polynomial regression (or dummies in categorical)

The matrix is unpacked, much like a categorical variable into a dummy. You get something like: y ~ Column1 + Column2 + Column3 + Column4 + Column5

Code 
i_knots <- c(-5, 0, 5)
basis_mat <- bs(x, knots = i_knots, degree = 1, intercept = TRUE)
lm1 <- lm(y ~ 0 + basis_mat, data = df) 
summary(lm1)

Are these slopes or are these tent positions?

You can think of these as a scaling factor. How tall does the first tent need to be, then how tall the second tent needs to be and so on

Code 
plot_linear

Raw data

Code 
library(splines)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(gridExtra) 

set.seed(123)
x <- seq(0, 10, length.out = 100)
y <- 3 * sin(x / 1.5) + 2 + rnorm(100, sd = 0.5)
data_df <- data.frame(x = x, y = y)
knots <- c(2.5, 5, 7.5)
B <- bs(x, knots = knots, degree = 1, intercept = TRUE)
model <- lm(y ~ 0 + B) 
coeffs <- coef(model)  
raw_basis_df <- as.data.frame(B)
raw_basis_df$x <- x
raw_long <- pivot_longer(raw_basis_df, cols = 1:5, names_to = "Tent", values_to = "Height")
scaled_B <- B %*% diag(coeffs)
scaled_df <- as.data.frame(scaled_B)
scaled_df$x <- x
scaled_long <- pivot_longer(scaled_df, cols = 1:5, names_to = "Tent", values_to = "Height")
coeff_df <- data.frame(
  Tent = paste0("V", 1:5),
  Coefficient = as.numeric(coeffs)
)
p1 <- ggplot(raw_long, aes(x = x, y = Height, color = Tent)) +
  geom_line(size = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = knots, linetype = "dotted") +
  labs(title = "1. The Raw Basis Functions", 
       subtitle = "Every tent has max height = 1.0",
       y = "Basis Value") +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "none")

p2 <- ggplot(coeff_df, aes(x = Tent, y = Coefficient, fill = Tent)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(Coefficient, 1)), vjust = -0.5) +
  labs(title = "2. The Coefficients", 
       y = "Coefficient Value") +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "none")

p3 <- ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = data_df, aes(x = x, y = y), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_area(data = scaled_long, aes(x = x, y = Height, fill = Tent), 
            alpha = 0.5, position = "identity") +
  geom_line(data = data.frame(x=x, y=predict(model)), aes(x=x, y=y), 
            size = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "3. The Weighted Tents", 
       subtitle = "Tent Height = Coefficient Value",
       y = "Y Value") +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "none")

p4 <-ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = data_df, aes(x = x, y = y), alpha = 0.7)+
  theme_minimal() 


p4

Code 
basis_df <- as.data.frame(basis_mat2)
basis_df$x <- x
basis_long <- pivot_longer(basis_df, cols = -x, names_to = "Basis", values_to = "Value")

ggplot(basis_long, aes(x = x, y = Value, color = Basis)) +
  geom_line(size = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = knots, linetype = "dashed", alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(title = paste("Basis Functions with", length(i_knots), "Internal Knots"),
       subtitle = paste("Total Basis Functions =", ncol(basis_mat2))) +
  theme_minimal()

Basis functions. We are describing many different “hills”, asking how much does this specific hill overlap with this specific data point? For every data point we are dividing up the hills into a probability that is equal to 1.

B is the basis and tells us where the hills are.

\(\beta_j\) tells us how tall the hills are (weights)

Multiplying together tells us the Weighted shapes

\[y = f(X)\] \[ y = \sum_{j=1}^{k} \beta_j B_j(X)\]

Code 
scaled_basis <- basis_mat2 %*% diag(coefs)
basis_df <- as.data.frame(scaled_basis)
basis_df$x <- x
basis_df$Total_Curve <- rowSums(scaled_basis) 

basis_long <- basis_df %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("V"), names_to = "Basis_Function", values_to = "Value")

ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = data_df, aes(x = x, y = y), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_area(data = basis_long, aes(x = x, y = Value, fill = Basis_Function), 
            alpha = 0.5, position = "identity") +
  geom_line(data = basis_df, aes(x = x, y = Total_Curve), 
            color = "black", size = 1.5, linetype = "solid") +
  labs(title = "Anatomy of a Spline",
       subtitle = "Colored Areas = Weighted Basis Functions \nBlack Line = The Combination ",
       y = "Y") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

Here the coefficients represent the Height of a Control Point or Magnet

Code 
n_coeffs <- length(coefs)
scaffold_x <- seq(min(x), max(x), length.out = n_coeffs)
scaffold_df <- data.frame(
  x = scaffold_x,
  y = as.numeric(coefs),
  Type = "Control Point (Coefficient)"
)

scaffold_df |> 
ggplot(aes(x=x, y=y)) +
geom_point( alpha = 0.3) +
 geom_line(linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
   geom_point(data = data_df, aes(x = x, y = y), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_area(data = basis_long, aes(x = x, y = Value, fill = Basis_Function), 
            alpha = 0.5, position = "identity") +
  geom_line(data = basis_df, aes(x = x, y = Total_Curve), 
            color = "black", alpha = .5, size = 1.5, linetype = "solid") + theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

  • The “scaled basis function” represented by the shaded hills tells you how much each basis function is influencing the model.

  • Can think about it as for any value of x, the height of the curve is represented by weighted values of different basis functions roughly such that the main hill corresponds to 66% of the height while the left and right contribute ~ 16%

  • These will be helpful in diagnosing over and under fitting.

50 knots

Code 
set.seed(123)
x <- seq(0, 10, length.out = 100)
y <- sin(x) + rnorm(100, sd = 0.2)
df <- data.frame(x = x, y = y)
basis_matrix <- bs(x, df = 50, intercept = TRUE) 
model <- lm(y ~ basis_matrix - 1) 
coeffs <- coef(model)
scaled_basis <- basis_matrix %*% diag(coeffs)
basis_df <- as.data.frame(scaled_basis)
basis_df$x <- x
basis_df$Total_Curve <- rowSums(scaled_basis) 
basis_long <- basis_df %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("V"), names_to = "Basis_Function", values_to = "Value")


n_coeffs <- length(coeffs)
scaffold_x <- seq(min(x), max(x), length.out = n_coeffs)
scaffold_df <- data.frame(
  x = scaffold_x,
  y = as.numeric(coeffs),
  Type = "Control Point (Coefficient)"
)


a50<- ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = df, aes(x = x, y = y), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_area(data = basis_long, aes(x = x, y = Value, fill = Basis_Function), 
            alpha = 0.5, position = "identity") +
  geom_line(data = basis_df, aes(x = x, y = Total_Curve), 
            color = "black", size = 1.5, linetype = "solid") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")


b50<- ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = df, aes(x = x, y = y), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_area(data = basis_long, aes(x = x, y = Value, fill = Basis_Function), 
            alpha = 0.5, position = "identity") +
  geom_line(data = basis_df, aes(x = x, y = Total_Curve), 
            color = "black", alpha = .4, size = 1.5, linetype = "solid") +
geom_point(data = scaffold_df, aes(x = x, y = y),alpha = 0.3) +
 geom_line(data = scaffold_df, aes(x = x, y = y), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(data = scaffold_df, aes(x = x, y = y), size = 3)  +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") 



a50

Basis dimensions

  • Low number results in less wiggliness. May be under fit

  • High number results in more wiggliness. May over fit.

Cherry blossom data

Code 
library(rethinking)
data(cherry_blossoms)
d <- cherry_blossoms
rm(cherry_blossoms)

knots

Code 
d2 <-
  d %>% 
  drop_na(doy)

num_knots <- 15
knot_list <- quantile(d2$year, probs = seq(from = 0, to = 1, length.out = num_knots))

d %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = doy)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = knot_list, color = "white", alpha = 1/2) +
  geom_point(color = "#ffb7c5", alpha = 1/2) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#4f455c"),
        panel.grid = element_blank())

      family = gaussian,

                prior(exponential(1), class = sigma)),
      iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, chains = 4, cores = 4,
      seed = 4,
      backend = "cmdstanr",
      file = "spline")

GAMs

  • Offer a solution to the regression spline issue of how many knots should we fit by utilizing penalized (regularized) splines. Fit lots of basis function, see if it improved the fit.

  • GAMs offer a middle ground from simple lines to localized lowess curves: they can be fit to complex, nonlinear relationships and make good predictions in these cases, but we are still able to do inferential statistics and understand and explain the underlying structure of our models

Generalized additive models

Similar to going from general linear model to generalized linear model. One more generalization.

\[y \sim ExpoFam(\mu, etc.)\]

\[ \mu = f(x) \] Instead of one coefficient per predictor, in GAMs we have many.

\[f(x) = \sum_{j=1}^{k} \beta_j \cdot B_j(x)\]

actual gam model

spline2 <-
  brm(data = d2,
      family = gaussian,
      doy ~ 1 + s(year),
      prior = c(prior(normal(100, 10), class = Intercept),
                prior(normal(0, 10), class = b),
                prior(student_t(3, 0, 5.9), class = sds),
                prior(exponential(1), class = sigma)),
      iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, chains = 4, cores = 4,
      seed = 4,
      control = list(adapt_delta = .99),
      backend = "cmdstanr",
      file = "spline2")

personality <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/josh-jackson/longitudinal-2022/main/Subject_personality.csv")

personality<- personality %>% 
  group_by(mapid) %>%
  arrange(neodate) %>% 
  dplyr::mutate(wave = seq_len(n())) 

personality$neodate <- as.Date(personality$neodate, origin = "1900-01-01")
personality.wide <- personality %>% 
  dplyr::select(mapid, wave, neodate) %>% 
  spread(wave, neodate) 

personality.wide$wave_1 <- personality.wide$'1'
personality.wide$wave_2 <- personality.wide$'2'
personality.wide$wave_3 <- personality.wide$'3'
personality.wide$wave_4 <- personality.wide$'4'
personality.wide$wave_5 <- personality.wide$'5'

personality.wide <- personality.wide %>% 
mutate (w_1 = (wave_1 - wave_1)/365,
          w_2 = (wave_2 - wave_1)/365,
          w_3 = (wave_3 - wave_1)/365,
          w_4 = (wave_4 - wave_1)/365,
        w_5 = (wave_5 - wave_1)/365)

personality.long <- personality.wide %>% 
  dplyr::select(mapid, w_1:w_5) %>% 
  gather(wave, year, -mapid) %>% 
  separate(wave, c('weeks', 'wave' ), sep="_") %>% 
 dplyr::select(-weeks) 

personality.long$wave <-  as.numeric(personality.long$wave)


personality <- personality %>% 
   left_join(personality.long, by = c('mapid', 'wave' )) 

personality.s <- personality %>% 
  group_by(mapid) %>% 
  tally() %>% 
   filter(n >=2) 

 personality <- personality %>% 
   filter(mapid %in% personality.s$mapid)

 personality <- personality %>% 
  mutate(year = as.numeric(year))

personality <- personality %>% 
  select(-neodate)

EDF

  • Effective Degrees of Freedom (EDF) represents the complexity or wiggliness of a smooth term.

  • An EDF of 1 indicates a linear relationship, edf of ~2 looks roughly like a quadratic shape. >3 gets more wiggly.

types of smoothing functions

Basis Type R Code Pro and con Best Use Case
Thin Plate bs="tp" No manual knots but slow Default choice
B-Spline bs="bs" Simple but requires knots Know knot locations
Factor Smooth bs="fs" Separate curve per subject Longitudinal studies
Random Effect bs="re" Treats variable as random intercept/slope. Hierarchical models

thin plate

  • Cubic splines can be tricky when data do not exist between knots as they are “local” whereas tp looks at entire dataset at once.
  • Is focused on distance between data points, \(r\), with a basis fucntion of: \(r^2 \log(r)\).
  • But this results in # basis functions = datapoints, which make it computationally expensive.
  • Uses Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to reduce to the most important functions ~ 10

Code 
x_val <- seq(0, 10, length.out = 200)
df <- data.frame(x = x_val, y = rnorm(200))
sm_bs <- smoothCon(s(x, bs = "bs", k = 9), data = df, absorb.cons = FALSE)[[1]]
df_bs <- as.data.frame(sm_bs$X) 
colnames(df_bs) <- paste0("Basis_", 1:ncol(df_bs))
df_bs$x <- x_val
df_bs$Type <- "Cubic B-Spline"

sm_tp <- smoothCon(s(x, bs = "tp", k = 9), data = df, absorb.cons = TRUE)[[1]]
df_tp <- as.data.frame(sm_tp$X)
colnames(df_tp) <- paste0("Basis_", 1:ncol(df_tp))
df_tp$x <- x_val
df_tp$Type <- "Thin Plate Spline"

mod_tp <- gam(y ~ s(x, bs = "tp", k = 9), data = df)
mat_tp <- predict(mod_tp, type = "lpmatrix")
df_tp <- as.data.frame(mat_tp[, -1])
colnames(df_tp) <- paste0("Basis_", 1:ncol(df_tp))
df_tp$x <- x_val
df_tp$Type <- "Thin Plate Spline (Global Waves)"

plot_data <- bind_rows(df_bs, df_tp) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("Basis_"), 
               names_to = "Basis_Function", 
               values_to = "Value")

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = x, y = Value, color = Basis_Function)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~Type, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
  labs(title = "B-Splines are local. Thin Plate Splines are global.",
       x = "X Variable", y = "Raw Basis Function Value") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        strip.text = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
        strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey90"))

Interactions

Thin Plate are “isotropic” meaning the independent variables are assumed to be on the same scale. So things get tricky with interactions.

s(x, z, bs = 'tp')

#tensor product smooths (really just cubic)
te(x, z) or t2(x, z) or s(x) + s(z) + ti(x, z)

Random effects and factor smooths

  • Based on description, both are applicable for longitudinal models.

  • Differences are in the geometry. re penalizes the magnitude while fs penalizes the magnitude and geometry.

  • re: differ in baseline/slope fs: differ in their entire trajectory

  • With 4 or less, need to use re. But with large data fitting unique curves with fs may cause computation problems

Penalized estimation

  • One concern is that we overfit our data and make our lines too wiggly. We can overcome this via penalized estimation, basically balancing minimizing residuals with out of sample prediction.

\[\mathcal{L}_p = \log(\text{Likelihood}) - \lambda W\]

  • Lambda is a penalization parameter and W is our wiggliness parameter. It is the second derivative of our curve. The rate of change of the rate of change

  • In mgcv, a penalization parameter often called lambda uses cross validation to balance over vs under fitting. It modifies the loss function to approximate leave-one-out cross-validation selection.

  • As λ increases, the result is a linear fit because any wiggliness will add too much to the loss function. As λ decreases closer to zero, wiggliness is incorporated into the model.

Longitudinal models

  • How unique?

  • Need to think about what we want to vary. Prior we varied intercepts and slopes. But they were relatively low rank so it is easy to think in terms of how people differed in amount

  • We now have more options in terms of wiggliness. Can people’s shapes be completely different? What about the wiggliness? People’s shapes are governed by the fixed effect in our previous models, should that still hold true here?

      geom_line(alpha = .2)

GAMs penalize the second derivative, shrinking curves toward a straight, flat line. By setting m=1, we penalize the first derivative, which shrinks the individual subject curves toward the global curve. It essentially tells the model: “Make the subjects look like the global average, unless they have strong data proving otherwise.”

Need more timepoints, and wiggliness

Code 
set.seed(74) 
n_subjects <- 20
n_timepoints <- 10
df <- expand.grid(
  time = 1:n_timepoints,
  id = factor(1:n_subjects)
)

subjects <- data.frame(
  id = factor(1:n_subjects),
  Profile = c(rep("Smooth", 10), rep("Volatile", 10)),
  Base_Int = rnorm(n_subjects, mean = 50, sd = 10),
  Base_Slope = rnorm(n_subjects, mean = 1, sd = 2),
  Wiggle_Amp = c(rep(0, 10), runif(10, 8, 15)),   
  Wiggle_Freq = c(rep(0, 10), runif(10, 1.2, 2.5)) 
)

data.sim <- df %>%
  left_join(subjects, by = "id") %>%
  mutate(
    Y = Base_Int + (Base_Slope * time) + (Wiggle_Amp * sin(Wiggle_Freq * time)) + rnorm(n(), 0, 2)
  )

ggplot(data.sim, aes(x = time, y = Y, group = id, color = Profile)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~Profile) +
  labs(x = "Wave", y = "DV") +
  theme_bw() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

factor smooths

  • The basis function coefficients partially pooled toward the mean

  • If the group overall is fairly smooth, \(\lambda\) goes up. This shared penalty acts like a gravitational pull, dragging everyone’s individual wiggles back toward the global trajectory.

Pooling with FS

Code 
set.seed(123)
time_seq <- seq(0, 10, length.out = 50)
df_normal <- expand.grid(Time = time_seq, ID = factor(1:18))
df_normal$True_Y <- 2 * df_normal$Time 
df_normal$Y <- df_normal$True_Y + rnorm(nrow(df_normal), 0, 2)

wild_trajectory <- function(t) { 2 * t + 6 * sin(1.5 * t) }

df_high <- data.frame(Time = time_seq, ID = factor("High_Data"))
df_high$True_Y <- wild_trajectory(df_high$Time)
df_high$Y <- df_high$True_Y + rnorm(50, 0, 1.5)

df_low <- data.frame(Time = c(2, 5, 8), ID = factor("Low_Data"))
df_low$True_Y <- wild_trajectory(df_low$Time)
df_low$Y <- df_low$True_Y + rnorm(3, 0, 1.5)

df_sim <- bind_rows(df_normal, df_high, df_low)
df_sim$ID <- as.factor(df_sim$ID)

mod_tug <- gam(Y ~ s(Time) + s(Time, ID, bs="fs", m=1), data = df_sim)

global_grid <- data.frame(Time = time_seq, ID = factor("High_Data")) 
global_grid$Pred_Global <- predict(mod_tug, newdata = global_grid, exclude = "s(Time,ID)")

specials_grid <- expand.grid(Time = time_seq, ID = factor(c("High_Data", "Low_Data")))
specials_grid$Pred_Individual <- predict(mod_tug, newdata = specials_grid)
specials_grid$True_Trajectory <- wild_trajectory(specials_grid$Time)


plot_data <- specials_grid %>% left_join(global_grid %>% select(Time, Pred_Global), by = "Time")
raw_points <- df_sim %>% filter(ID %in% c("High_Data", "Low_Data"))

Is it wiggliness or is it noise?

  • Thus far we have been working with gams which are different from multi-level or hierarchical gams. When would we need those? When we want to relax the assumption of zero correlation across time points.

  • If you ignore this assumption, your model will think it has more independent pieces of information than it actually does. The penalty (\(\lambda\)) will be too loose, the curves will overfit the noise.

  • Time-series data has “memory,” in that observations tend to be correleated such that if you overshoot your predicted trajectory at one timepoint, you are likely to be at the next timepoint.

Code 
data.sim <- data.sim %>%
  arrange(id, time) %>%
  mutate(start_point = time == min(time))

mod_ar1 <- bam(Y ~ s(time) + s(time, id, bs="fs", m=1, k=7),
               data = data.sim, 
               rho = 0.4,                 # The AR1 correlation parameter
               AR.start = start_point,    # Resets the AR1 process for each new subject
               method = "fREML")
summary(mod_ar1)
